title: Pembrolizumab + carboplatin/paclitaxel → AC

agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: PD-1 is a control switch on T cells, a type of immune cell. When it connects with PD-L1 or PD-L2, the T cell receives a signal to reduce its activity. Some cancers use this pathway to escape immune attack. Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, helping T cells recognise and attack the cancer. It does not directly poison cancer cells like chemotherapy. Releasing this brake can also allow immune cells to attack healthy organs, which explains the different side-effect pattern and why symptoms can appear after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver, kidneys or skin
Rare serious heart or neurological inflammation
Effects can first appear after treatment ends

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin creates links in DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic instructions. Its dose depends on kidney function as well as the intended regimen.
agents.watch: Keep blood-test appointments. Fever, unusual bleeding, repeated vomiting or infusion symptoms need prompt advice.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Allergic reaction, sometimes after previous exposure

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Hair loss, muscle or joint pain
Mouth, bowel, skin and nail effects

agents.name: Doxorubicin
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk.
agents.watch: Report pain or burning at the infusion site immediately. New breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt review. Red urine for a short time can be a drug-colour effect; pain, clots or persistent bleeding still need advice.
risks: Low counts, infection and mouth ulcers
Severe tissue injury if the infusion leaks

agents.name: Cyclophosphamide
agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
agents.watch: Use the prescribed anti-sickness and hydration plan. Report fever, painful urination or blood in the urine.

context_label: Triple-negative early breast cancer · before and after surgery
purpose: This pathway combines immunotherapy, chemotherapy and surgery to reduce recurrence risk in eligible high-risk early triple-negative breast cancer.
schedule_summary: Cycles 1–4: pembrolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1; paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15. Cycles 5–8: pembrolizumab + doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC) on Day 1 every 21 days. Surgery is followed by pembrolizumab when appropriate.

phases_note: A general pathway, not an appointment calendar. Your team confirms the order, overlap and duration; no date entry is needed.
timeline_note: Treatment bands show the source schedule. Symptom bands show possible patterns, not measured probabilities; serious effects can occur at any time.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
teachback: Can you explain the current phase, which checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today? You do not need to enter dates to read the plan.
consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions, the planned monitoring and who to contact. Review the full longitudinal pathway and confirm which conditional treatments apply.
urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

support.title: The phase matters
support.text: Premedicines, anti-sickness medicines and growth-factor plans may change when paclitaxel/carbo changes to AC.

support.title: Immune safety
support.text: Report new diarrhoea, breathlessness, rash, headache or marked fatigue, including after treatment ends.

support.title: Access and visits
support.text: Weekly visits in phase 1; every-three-week AC visits in phase 2. There is no routine home chemotherapy pump.

support.title: Recovery and fertility
support.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment and ask about scalp cooling, exercise and practical support.

questions.q: How does this fit around surgery and radiotherapy?
questions.a: This is NCCP 00857: four 3-week cycles of carboplatin/weekly paclitaxel with pembrolizumab, then four 3-week AC cycles with pembrolizumab, surgery, and postoperative pembrolizumab when appropriate.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. Both charts explain the expected sequence and general intervals without any dates or personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments.
The treatment journey lists baseline and ongoing checks, why they matter and what to ask. It does not mark tests as booked or completed.

questions.q: What happens if treatment is delayed?
questions.a: Your team may delay, reduce, change or stop a medicine. Ask which component changes and what happens to the next review; do not restart independently.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy or breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. The team should explain contraception and breastfeeding restrictions for every medicine, including how long precautions continue afterwards.

questions.q: How should I use trial numbers?
questions.a: Trial results describe groups with defined eligibility. Ask how well those patients and their treatment match your situation; the figures are not an individual prediction.

evidence.title: KEYNOTE-522: five-year overall survival
evidence.intro: The treatment setting, trial population and endpoint matter when interpreting benefit.
evidence.population: The randomised phase III trial enrolled 1,174 patients with previously untreated stage II–III triple-negative breast cancer.
evidence.interpretation: At five years, the estimated proportions alive were 86.6% and 81.7%, an absolute difference of 4.9 percentage points. These are trial-group estimates for the full before-and-after-surgery strategy, not a prediction for one person. The study allowed chemotherapy variants; use the exact NCCP 00857 schedule for this card.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim
chapters.intro: Confirm the setting and the plan.

items.title: Why this regimen?
items.text: This pathway combines immunotherapy, chemotherapy and surgery to reduce recurrence risk in eligible high-risk early triple-negative breast cancer.

items.title: The larger pathway
items.text: This is NCCP 00857: four 3-week cycles of carboplatin/weekly paclitaxel with pembrolizumab, then four 3-week AC cycles with pembrolizumab, surgery, and postoperative pembrolizumab when appropriate.

items.title: Know when the chemotherapy changes
items.text: After four 3-week cycles. The weekly paclitaxel visits stop and the AC phase starts. Confirm which medicines and supportive medicines change.

items.title: Thyroid and other immune checks
items.text: Thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks; glucose each cycle; other tests as indicated. Pembrolizumab can inflame hormone glands and other organs. Report diarrhoea, breathlessness, severe fatigue, thirst, headache, rash or jaundice promptly.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Ask for support that fits your priorities.

chapters.title: When treatment changes or finishes
chapters.intro: The next phase has its own checks.

items.title: Know the continuing plan
items.text: Annual mammography of remaining breast tissue after treatment; the team sets the first date. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. New symptoms need assessment between visits. Report new symptoms early, including after immunotherapy has stopped.

items.title: Keep reporting symptoms
items.text: New or lasting symptoms need assessment between appointments and after treatment stops. Ask for a written summary of continuing medicines, follow-up tests and the contact plan.

phases.label: Cycles 1–4: weekly paclitaxel phase
phases.detail: Pembrolizumab 200 mg and carboplatin AUC5 on Day 1, with paclitaxel 80 mg/m² on Days 1, 8 and 15 of each 21-day cycle.

phases.label: Cycles 5–8: AC phase
phases.detail: Pembrolizumab 200 mg with doxorubicin 60 mg/m² and cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m² on Day 1 every 21 days.

phases.label: After surgery: pembrolizumab
phases.detail: After surgery, pembrolizumab may continue for 9 doses of 200 mg every 3 weeks or 5 doses of 400 mg every 6 weeks. This later schedule is shown in the whole-treatment map, not as extra drugs in the 21-day chemotherapy chart.

day_groups.title: Follow the phase and prescribed schedule
day_groups.body: Cycles 1–4: pembrolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1; paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15. Cycles 5–8: pembrolizumab + doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC) on Day 1 every 21 days. Surgery is followed by pembrolizumab when appropriate.
day_groups.action: Keep planned tests and call for symptoms at any time.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment days
chronology_notes.text: Cycles 1–4: pembrolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1; paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15. Cycles 5–8: pembrolizumab + doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC) on Day 1 every 21 days. Surgery is followed by pembrolizumab when appropriate.

chronology_notes.title: Read the phase labels
chronology_notes.text: Only the medicines in your current phase apply. The chart is an overview, not an instruction to combine phases.

chronology_notes.title: The bigger picture
chronology_notes.text: Use the whole-treatment journey for surgery, radiation, scans and longer-term checks.

logistics.title: Your practical treatment plan
logistics.intro: Cycles 1–4: pembrolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1; paclitaxel on Days 1, 8 and 15. Cycles 5–8: pembrolizumab + doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC) on Day 1 every 21 days. Surgery is followed by pembrolizumab when appropriate.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, cardiac/immune checks as relevant, medicines review and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Trained staff check and access the line, give the prescribed premedicines and infusions, and monitor for reactions. Tell the nurse immediately about pain, burning, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

anatomy: Hair loss or thinning varies. Ask about support and scalp cooling where appropriate.
Painful ulcers or difficulty eating and drinking need advice.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment.
Fainting, chest pain or severe breathing difficulty: urgent help. Keep scheduled cardiac checks.
Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor fluid intake, pain or fever.
Report lasting numbness, painful joints or difficulty with daily activities.
Fever, shivers or suddenly unwell: contact oncology immediately.
Severe rash, blistering or yellow skin/eyes needs prompt advice.
